summary:
We built Fire in Microgravity: Evidence Explorer, an open-source, AI-assisted dashboard that ranks, compares and interprets NASA flame experiments for a chosen mission. A planner sets gravity (0 g, lunar, Mars or Earth), cabin atmosphere and hazards of concern. The tool ranks 17 experiments with a transparent five-part score, compares them side by side, maps evidence by material and environment, and shows where evidence is missing. Claude writes briefings and answers questions only from retrieved records, cites a source for every claim, labels its own reasoning, and says “insufficient evidence” when the records cannot answer.

This addresses the challenge’s call to summarize, rank and interpret NASA’s microgravity combustion findings for fire safety. It matters because NASA screens materials at 1 g, yet partial-gravity studies suggest lunar gravity may be among the most flammable conditions, and the partial-gravity evidence we found comes only from aircraft, drop towers and centrifuges. Artemis-era habitats need fire-safety decisions grounded in cited evidence, with the gaps made visible.
details:
What it does and how it works

Fire safety for the Moon and Mars depends on evidence scattered across many NASA flame experiments. Our dashboard turns that evidence into a decision tool. A mission planner sets gravity (0 g, lunar, Mars or Earth), the cabin atmosphere and the hazards they care about. The tool ranks 17 experiments and studies from NASA’s ISS, Saffire and SoFIE work, drop towers, parabolic flights and ground tests. Each experiment gets a score built from five adjustable parts: scenario match, hazard focus, cabin materials, evidence quality and recency. It can compare experiments side by side, map evidence by material and environment, and list the hazards with no direct evidence for the chosen scenario. Claude writes mission briefings and answers questions, but only from the retrieved records. It must cite a record for every claim, label its own reasoning as “Interpretation”, and say “insufficient evidence” when the records can’t answer.

Why it matters

The catalogue brings out the gap this challenge is about. NASA screens spacecraft materials at 1 g, yet partial-gravity studies suggest lunar gravity may be among the most flammable conditions. In our catalogue, the partial-gravity evidence comes only from aircraft, drop towers and centrifuges, with seconds of test time. The dashboard makes that gap visible, so fire-safety planning for Artemis-era habitats can rest on cited evidence and show where more testing is needed.

What makes it creative

  • A gravity slider drives both a flame illustration and the evidence coverage.
  • The design starts from gaps rather than results.
  • Every finding is labelled Reported, Description or Interpretation, and links to its source.

Tools and methods

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the dashboard.
  • Python for the scoring, the data pipeline and an optional FastAPI server.
  • Claude (Anthropic) for briefings, cited Q&A and record extraction.
  • Data: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics combustion datasets, NASA Technical Reports Server papers, and published Saffire, BASS-II and SoFIE results. All are listed in the references.
  • Testing: the Python and browser scores match, and the data pipeline keeps a tag only if its supporting quote appears verbatim in the source.

What we considered

  • Evidence is labelled by how reliable it is.
  • Limits are stated plainly: the catalogue is hand-built from NASA documents with coarse tags, not parsed from raw PSI files.
  • Scores rank how relevant the evidence is, not fire risk.
  • The project is open source under Apache-2.0.

AI use: Claude helped write the code, the catalogue text and the pipeline, and powers the live briefing and Q&A features
dataRefs: NASA PSI combustion datasets (BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, DAFT, ACME)
NASA PSI Users Group: FLEX cool-flame results
projectRefs: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment
